statement: Week 3, day 1 of the course is all about distributed systems; the next class (tomorrow) covers distributed ID generators.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: tomorrow we'll be discussing distributed ID generators

statement: Distributed systems was one of the most neglected subjects during the teacher's bachelor's and master's (no one wanted to take it), yet once people enter industry, distributed systems are everywhere.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: No one wanted to take that subject. But as soon as they enter industry, oh my God, distributed systems are everywhere.

statement: The core algorithms discussed in the literature are the theoretical foundation; when real systems are discussed, you see how beautifully those pieces fit into place.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what we are taught is a theoretical foundation for it

statement: The first agenda item is how to approach designing a distributed system (not the theory); there is no secret sauce and only one thing to remember to build good systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when you are designing a system, how should you approach it? And there is no secret sauce.

statement: The load balancer is typically the core component that makes distributed systems possible, because it abstracts away the details of having multiple servers in the backend.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the core component that makes distributed systems possible is typically a load balancer, because it is what is abstracting the details

statement: The class goes through a very realistic load balancer design and briefly through the source code of a tiny load balancer the teacher wrote, to understand the core implementation logic rather than just drawing boxes.
detail: The teacher's load balancer is in no way productionizable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: we'll go through the source code of a very tiny load balancer that I created. In no way it is productionizable

statement: Drawing boxes is something anyone can do; understanding the granular implementation detail is the differentiating factor.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: drawing boxes is two-year-old kid can do that. Understanding this granular detail is the differentiating factor.

statement: Writing a load balancer is simple: hardly 10 lines of core code; most people never think of writing one, but an engineer wrote NGINX, which people use as a reverse proxy.
detail: The teacher says even '10 lines' is an exaggeration.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We would see how simple it is to build a load balancer. Hardly 10 lines of core code.

statement: After the break, the class discusses remote and distributed locking.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: post that we would be having discussions around remote and distributed locking

statement: Distributed locking is needed because multiple processes must coordinate among themselves to keep data consistent; e.g. two distributed transactions both trying to update the same row, where one must stop the other from updating.
detail: In a distributed setup (not a single database) many more challenges come in.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: imagine you have multiple processors and they have to coordinate among themselves so that the data consistency thing stays in check.

statement: Remote locks and distributed locks form the heart and crux of data correctness and consistency in distributed systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: remote locks and distributed locks, they form the heart and crux of data correctness and consistency in distributed systems

statement: The locking discussion first answers why you need a lock (the more important question), then how to implement it using Redis.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: first of all, why you need it. That's a more important question to answer. And then how do you implement it using Redis?

statement: Beyond Redis, what matters is the core property a system needs in order to act as a lock manager, so you could build your own; understanding the core access pattern and the core ways of building it is what matters.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: what's the core property that we see from a system that could be a lock manager

statement: Last week database locking was taught with an airline check-in system example; distributed locking is taught with a (very hypothetical) synchronization example.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: last week in order to understand database locking, we took an example of online offline, we took an example of airline check-in system

statement: Pre-reads are not shared on the Discord channel: it was tried, but the flood of links made the channel inactive and people missed interesting messages; pre-reads come by email every Sunday and are on the platform beneath the video.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it made channel very inactive because there is a lot of links links links links, so you tend to miss out on interesting messages

statement: This is the teacher's 16th course; the course format has evolved by experiments across batches ('natural selection'), keeping what works.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is my 16th course.

statement: To keep focus in sessions longer than an hour (all sessions run 2+ hours): keep your phone in a different room and keep pen and paper handy to scribble notes.
detail: The teacher always took notes in long lectures and never lost focus.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: One thing that I always tell is have a pen paper handy.

statement: Sessions are not split into parts: the teacher tried it in cohorts 7, 8 and 9 and it broke concentration; the context must be set up again and people who leave on a break often never come back.
detail: Example: the Slack discussion ran an hour and a half.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I did break it 7th, 8th and 9th cohort. I tried that. But what happened was it was a break in concentration for most.

statement: Take notes physically with pen and paper rather than typing, because a browser opens the door to Twitter, Instagram, WhatsApp and other distractions.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Physically doing it and not typing

statement: In the real world design discussions go on for three or four hours straight; covering a system needs to happen in one shot (e.g. a roughly two-hour S3 discussion without a break), since re-setting the context costs about 20 minutes.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you would see design discussions going for three hours, four hours straight

statement: The teacher will add breaks in two systems he has in mind and will announce when.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But I have two systems in mind where I will be taking those breaks.

statement: 'Distributed systems' is one of the most misused terms in the age of social media; people call anything a distributed system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is one of the most misused term in the age of social media

statement: A distributed system gives you the ability to abstract out the distributedness: to an outsider it is one single coherent system, while behind it a huge set of machines each do their job.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it gives you an ability to abstract out the distributedness of the system

statement: The 'outsider' who sees one coherent system is contextual: it may be an end user, a microservice or an internal portal; for them the complexity of running on different machines is abstracted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now outside is contextual, it may be end user, it may be some microservice, it may be some internal portal

statement: Facebook.com is just one website to users, and a college kid may think they can build Facebook, but at scale many different kinds of services must interact just to render a simple home feed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: how many different kinds of services need to interact with each other in order to just render a simple home feed

statement: As the teacher's master's professor (who published many distributed-systems papers) used to say: you fall in love with distributed systems if you understand them well, and you hate them when you understand them well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you'll fall in love with distributed systems if you understand it well and you will hate distributed systems when you understand it well.

statement: In distributed systems anything that could go wrong will go wrong (Murphy's law): a condition you think will never happen happens the next day and takes your system down; if you don't handle such scenarios you are not guaranteeing correctness.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: with distributed systems what happens is anything that could go wrong would go wrong.

statement: If things break during a distributed transaction and the data goes into an inconsistent state you did not consider while designing, you get data corruption; this is the part you hate.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Imagine while doing a distributed transaction things break and data go in an inconsistent state and you didn't consider it

statement: The part you love: when you start building a distributed system it is great, because you can scale horizontally.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But when you start building one, you would find it very happy.

statement: The key idea for approaching distributed systems: assume anything and everything will go wrong, then check whether your code and system handle it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Assume anything and everything would go wrong.

statement: Always start with the day zero architecture and don't overcomplicate it: one machine, one server, one database, one cache.
detail: The teacher's own approach ('take it with a pinch of salt'), which worked extremely well for the truly distributed systems he designed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: always start with the day zero architecture. Always don't over complicate on day zero. One machine, one server, one database, one cache.

statement: After day zero: scale each component independently, see how it performs under load, rectify the system, re-architect, and repeat.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Then scale each component independently. See how it performs under load, rectify the system, re-architect and repeat.

statement: When you check how a system performs under load, the low-level details are the pain points; spend time understanding what happens at the code level, what is going wrong and how to fix it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Those low level details are the ones that are pain points.

statement: This is the incremental approach of system design (system design is about building distributed systems); in complex systems people always iterate this way: day zero, then scale step by step.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is mostly the incremental approach of system design

statement: Designing this way is like looking at a culture under a microscope: you zoom in, find something, zoom further into finer detail and see a whole new world; each time you zoom in on granular details and fix them.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's like literally you having a microscope and looking into a culture, and you are zooming in

statement: Many people think they have a distributed system when they just have a bunch of remote machines talking to each other; that is not a distributed system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: They just have a bunch of remote machines that are talking to each other. That's not distributed system.

statement: A distributed system is one that can handle scale with a large number of machines, but more importantly it must be horizontally scalable; this is precisely why you build distributed systems.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: A distributed system is what is able to handle a scale.

statement: Horizontal scalability does not come just from having more machines or auto-scaled API servers; think of every single layer of your architecture and check whether it is horizontally scalable.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Think of every single layer in your architecture and see if it is horizontal, is scalable or not.

statement: A layer that is not horizontally scalable is a single point of failure.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: If it is not, then that is a single point of failure.
flags: asr: [?single point of failure | asr: "single point of view"]

statement: Every component of the system you design needs to be horizontally scalable: database, cache, stateful services, stateless services, API servers, load balancer, CDN.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: every single one of the component in whatever system that you're designing needs to be horizontally scalable

statement: Horizontally scalable does not just mean having an auto-scaling policy that triggers and adds servers to handle load; it is much more than that.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: We just don't mean that we can just have an auto-scaling policy which gets triggered, you add more server to handle the load.

statement: Horizontal scalability implies knowing the unit economics of your service: how many requests each server can handle, which lets you do linear amplification; linear amplification is needed to build a good distributed system.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: how many requests each one of my server can handle? Depending on which you can do linear amplification.

statement: Without knowing per-server capacity you are playing with fire: adding machines without thought, leaking money, and either under-provisioning or over-provisioning.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Otherwise you are just playing with fire.

statement: Knowing how much load (API load, processing load, etc.) each machine can handle means you are not leaking money when scaling; understanding the unit economy of a single server is what a good distributed system is about.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Understanding the unit economy of a single server in your system.

statement: Per-server capacity varies with the service; understand the limitation of each server and make the system truly distributed across all layers (database, API server, everything), not just the API servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Understand the limitation of each server.

statement: In some cases you cut corners: e.g. not having a horizontally scalable database is perfectly fine as long as it can handle the load.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I will not have database as a horizontally scalable database, and it is perfectly fine so long as it is able to handle the load

statement: The teacher has changed load balancing algorithms in practice to get performance; the algorithms are discussed practically, not theoretically.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I've changed load balancing algorithm by like in order to get performance.

statement: The load balancer is the one rectangle box drawn in every system and assumed to work magically, but it is a piece of code someone wrote (e.g. hundreds of engineers wrote AWS's load balancers), so there is no reason to treat it as a black box.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: load balancer is this one rectangle box that we draw in every system.

statement: Approach building a load balancer from first principles, not just the core tech needed, to build raw intuition about building the system.
detail: Load balancers made life so simple that people take them for granted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: let's approach it from first principles so that we built a raw intuition around building the system

statement: Flipkart had to build its own load balancer because it runs private, on-premise infrastructure in its own data center (it can't be on Amazon, and migrating to GCP was a pain); you too may be put in a situation where you must write and scale your own load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Flipkart had to build their own load balancer because they are still having private infrastructure.

statement: A load balancer acts as a single point of entry: one domain name or IP address that does not change; anyone talking to the backend servers talks via the load balancer, so clients don't need to remember where to talk.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: load balancer acts as a single point of entry. So that is one domain name or one IP address that is not changing.

statement: It is the load balancer's responsibility to forward each request to one of the backend servers to get it handled.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's responsibility of load balancer to forward a request to one of the server to get it handled.

statement: The load balancing algorithm is the basis on which the load balancer decides which server to forward a request to; three are discussed (what they are, how and where to use them).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: on what basis would this load balancer decide which server to forward the request to? So this is load balancing algorithm.

statement: Round robin is the most common algorithm and the default in almost all load balancers: requests go across the backend servers in turn (1, 2, 3, 1, 2, ...).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: round robin is the most common one, which almost all load balancers default load balancing algorithm is round robin.

statement: For round robin the load balancer keeps track of which backend server it forwarded the last request to and forwards the next request to the next server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: load balancer keeps a track of, hey, where did I forward my last request to, which backend server?

statement: Use round robin when you have uniform infrastructure (e.g. every API server has 4 GB RAM) and a uniform load pattern.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You would use it when you have uniform infrastructure and uniform load pattern

statement: A uniform load pattern means that whatever API you hit, the result comes within a fixed time range (e.g. under one second), so response-time variance is low and it does not matter which server a request goes to.
detail: The teacher assumes homogeneous load here.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: no matter what API you hit, there is a fixed set of like time or a time range in which you can expect a result.

statement: With identical machines and low response-time variance, a request won't take very long on one server and very short on another, so sending requests one after another (round robin) distributes the load almost equally; it is the easiest scheme.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you can literally do round robin and distribute, almost distribute the load equally among the three servers

statement: Weighted round robin is round robin where you configure a weight for each machine and forward requests in proportion to the weights.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: weighted round robin is where you configure the weights of a machine.

statement: Example of non-uniform infrastructure behind a load balancer: three machines with 4 GB, 8 GB and 4 GB RAM, which can happen e.g. because you purchased reserved instances that lose money if unused.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have three machines, one with 4 GB RAM, second with 8 GB RAM, third with 4 GB RAM.

statement: With plain round robin on 4 GB / 8 GB / 4 GB machines, if the 4 GB machines run at 80% capacity the 8 GB machine (twice as many cores) runs at about 40%, because it gets the same share of requests; the infrastructure is under-utilized.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if these machines operate at 80% capacity, this machine would be operating at 40% capacity.

statement: With non-uniform infrastructure use weighted round robin; for 4 GB / 8 GB / 4 GB machines forward requests in the ratio 1:2:1, so the infrastructure is utilized well.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you forward the request in the ratio of 1 is to 2 is to 1

statement: Every load balancer offers a set of algorithms to pick from, each with its own configuration; check the official documentation of the load balancer you use to configure it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Every single load balancer that you use has a set of algorithms that you can pick from.

statement: If your cloud does not show the option to configure the load balancing algorithm (it may be behind a feature flag), raise a support ticket with the cloud provider; they have those options.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: reach out to your cloud provider, raise a support ticket, ask them you want to configure your load balancing algorithm.

statement: The teacher's team blundered by buying AWS reserved instances of different sizes, and AWS would not change them; instead of keeping them spare they put them into existing workloads and applied weighted round robin.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I actually configured weighted round because we made a blunder in purchasing reserved instances.

statement: The recurring pattern is money: an engineer must think about whether the infrastructure is being utilized well; if you don't care about money, the algorithm doesn't matter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: if you see the pattern over here, it's always about money.

statement: Putting a 60 GB RAM machine behind plain round robin is not efficient utilization of your resources.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Now put it 60 GB RAM machine and have a round robin.

statement: Saving money for your organization is how you make a quantified impact, which makes it easy to pitch for a promotion.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: try to save money for your organization, and that's how you can make a quantified impact.

statement: Only three load balancing algorithms are covered; the intuition for where to pick one can be applied to other algorithms as well.
detail: Least connections is one that a lot of people take for granted.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But you can see the intuition behind where to pick one. Similarly, you can apply for other algorithms as well.

statement: Least connections: when a request arrives, the load balancer checks which backend server has the fewest connections from the load balancer and forwards the request to it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: load balancer checks which of the backend server has least number of connections to the load balancer.

statement: Think of least connections like connection pooling for databases: the load balancer can create multiple connections to a server and tracks how many it has to each (it is not actually a connection pool; just an example).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: As we had connection pooling for databases, think of it in a similar way.

statement: The load balancer keeps track of how many active connections it has to each backend server; when a request completes its connection is freed, so a new request can go back to that server; each new request goes to the server with the fewest active connections.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the load balancer will keep track of how many active connections it has to the backend servers, each of the backend servers.

statement: Without connection pooling, an open connection means the server is busy: an HTTP connection from load balancer to backend is terminated when the server responds, so the more active connections a server has, the busier it is.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for the time the connections are active, it actually means the server is busy.
flags: unclear: "are load bands are made in"

statement: Least connections forwards a request to the machine that is least burdened at the moment, increasing the probability of quicker response times.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you are increasing the probability of you getting quicker response times.

statement: A high-variance workload: some APIs take one second, some one minute, some one hour; analytics is the classic case, where some queries answer in one second and others take one or two hours.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Some analytics queries give you answer in one second, some analytics queries give you answer in one hour

statement: Walkthrough under high variance: requests 1-3 go to servers 1-3; request 2 was a one-second request and finished, so request 4 goes to server 2 (fewest connections); if request 4 is long-running, request 5 then picks another server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the fourth request went to the second server

statement: With blunt round robin under high variance, long-running requests can all get scheduled onto one server that is already busy, bombarding it with more long-running work.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: all long running requests were just getting bogged onto this one server.

statement: When there is very large variance in the response or processing times of requests, use least connections, so each request is forwarded to a relatively free machine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it's better to go for least connections based approach. This way your request will be forwarded to a machine which is relatively free.

statement: The load balancer has no idea of a backend's CPU or memory, only of its network connections; the connection count is a rough estimate of how busy a backend is, which keeps the load balancer extremely stateless.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the beauty is load balancer does not have an idea of CPU or memory on this machine. All it has is idea of network connection.

statement: Letting the load balancer use backend CPU/memory usage to route is impractical: it would have to talk to another system, fire a query, look at historical usage and then decide, adding network latency and slowing things down; a load balancer needs to be lightning fast.
detail: Teacher calls 'I'll check the CPU usage of all of this' the most common random suggestion; don't make things too complicated there.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Load balancer needs to be lightning fast.

statement: Load balancing algorithms use heuristics because the routing decision must be made in microseconds, not even milliseconds; gathering CPU usage of all servers would add multiple milliseconds of latency.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you need to take decision right there and there in microseconds, not even milliseconds.

statement: Always think about practicality whenever you suggest a design idea.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Always think about practicality whenever you suggest something.

statement: A load balancer using least connections does not have to keep persistent connections to all machines: it can be completely stateless, or keep a connection pool, in which case it counts least ACTIVE connections (e.g. a pool of 100 with 2 in use = 2 active, 98 inactive).
detail: Asked by a student (Student 7); it's your code, so either way is fine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Either you go complete stateless or you keep a connection pool.

statement: A request can last an hour because it need not be plain HTTP: think raw TCP; a TCP connection never breaks by itself, only through a network interruption or the client or server terminating it.
detail: Student question: how does something that takes one hour happen over HTTP?
speaker: teacher
verbatim: TCP connection automatically never breaks off, right? Someone has to break it off.

statement: HTTP tells client and server to terminate the connection once the response arrives, but with keep-alive the connection can stay open; the teacher has had extremely long-running HTTP requests, but server-to-server, not from end users.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: But with keep-alive, you can still keep it open.

statement: gRPC is a classic example of a non-terminating connection: it works on top of HTTP/2 and the connection never terminates unless someone explicitly closes it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: gRPC, classic example, works on top of HTTP/2, the connection never terminates unless someone explicitly does that.

statement: A student worried that with least connections a fifth request may land on a server still busy with a long query while another is about to finish (the load balancer cannot know); the teacher answered that this assumes a server can handle only one query, and that you then need more servers.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Here you are assuming that a server can handle only one query.

statement: Least connections is a local optimization and that still works; no need for global optimization: with huge workloads you would have far more than three servers and just try to maximize execution across all requests.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Why would you want to go for global optimization? Local optimization still works.

statement: Data warehouses use least-connection-based balancing across clusters (per BigQuery / Redshift documentation), because a data warehouse classically mixes short-running and long-running queries.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is exactly what data warehouses do.

statement: If a user closes the browser and resubmits, the new request may go to another VM while the old job still runs; whether they get two results is business logic; with statefulness you must ensure the request reaches the same machine, but a TCP connection once broken is broken, so for this kind of work use asynchronous processing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: because it is TCP, once it's broken, it's broken.

statement: Once a job is submitted it is submitted: normal HTTP web servers don't give you tooling to stop it when the client goes away, but you can implement it, since when the TCP connection breaks you get notified on the socket.
detail: Possible if you control the underlying execution engine; normal web servers are open source and can be tweaked.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When the TCP breaks off, you get notified right on the socket that okay, the connection has gone on.

statement: Redshift and BigQuery let you cancel a very long-running query, which stops its execution.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That's what Redshift and BigQuery gives you. When you fire a very long running query, there is an option to cancel your run.

statement: The teacher built his first load balancer in Go around March 2021 (COVID time, at his in-laws') while preparing his first cohort, to show a real demo, and was thrilled when it first ran.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I built my load balancer. I'd use normal Golang to build one.

statement: The teacher's load balancer balanced load across servers with several algorithms: consistent hashing, round robin, weighted round robin and static routing.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: with consistent hashing, with round robin, weighted round robin, static routing and whatnot.

statement: Benchmarked against Nginx and HAProxy, the teacher's load balancer was 5x-6x faster than Nginx, but only because Nginx and HAProxy do much more than his simple load balancer, as he learned going deep into Nginx.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Mine was 5x or 6x faster than Nginx.

statement: Find time to implement everything you see; you will learn details most people don't know.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Find some time, implement everything.

statement: This cohort the load balancer is taught low-level first, then how it fits the high-level picture (other cohorts started high-level and ran out of time), including why one server cannot be the load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This time I want to start with low level details of it.

statement: LB server: the server running the load balancer; a load balancer is itself a process on a machine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the server that runs your load balancer is the LB server.

statement: Backend servers: the servers requests are forwarded to (e.g. payment service, auth service, profile service); they are a black box for the load balancer being built.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there are back-end servers, that's a payment service, auth service, profile service, those are your back-end servers.

statement: Spinning up a load balancer means a VM spins up running the load balancing process, which is a normal TCP server process (not even an HTTP server).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It's a normal TCP server's process, which is running over here in this machine.

statement: In the running example the single LB server has the static IP address 10.0.0.1, which does not change.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say 10.0.0.1. Now this is a static IP address. This IP address would not change.

statement: Start with a day zero architecture (a single LB machine); thinking about scale on day zero is the worst way to build a system; think simple.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Don't think of scale on day zero. Worst way to build a system. Think simple.

statement: The backend API servers run a normal HTTP server (Flask, Spring Boot, any framework) serving /index.html with 'hello world', listening on port 8081.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say they are running on 8081 port right now.

statement: To connect to any server you need its IP address and port number; in the example the three backends are 10.0.0.7, 10.0.0.8 and 10.0.0.9.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for anyone, anyone to connect to the server, you need IP address and port number.

statement: The load balancer stores a list of all backend servers (IP:port); this corresponds to the console configuration where you specify which servers are behind the load balancer.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say you have a list of all the backend servers.

statement: A client (a user or another server) sending a request to the load balancer means establishing a TCP connection with it, so the LB server must listen on a TCP port (e.g. 9000).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: when we say client sent a request, what does it mean? It means that the client established a TCP connection with the server.

statement: The request reaches the load balancer server because the client only has the load balancer's IP address.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: client only has IP address of load balancer server.

statement: The backend servers (Spring Boot, Flask, Django) accept HTTP requests on port 8081, and HTTP runs over TCP; forwarding is not just packet-level forwarding.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What they accept? HTTP request. What is HTTP? TCP request.

statement: On receiving a request, the LB server first picks a backend by its load balancing algorithm; with the simplest, a random strategy, it just picks one of the three at random.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Let's say I have a random balancing strategy. Let's keep it simple. Random.

statement: The LB server then creates a TCP connection to the chosen backend (e.g. 10.0.0.7:8081), so one client request involves two TCP connections: client to load balancer, and load balancer to backend server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So for one request from the client, there are two TCP connections that are set up.

statement: The LB server must keep a map of which source TCP connection (client to LB) is mapped to which target TCP connection (LB to backend).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: So which source TCP connection is mapped to which target TCP connection.

statement: Source TCP connection = between the client and the LB server; target TCP connection = between the load balancer and the backend server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is target TCP connection which is established between load balancer and backend server.

statement: This connection-mapping design is exactly how the teacher first thought of building a load balancer, applying first principles; there is nothing fancy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this is exactly how I thought of building a load balancer.

statement: The source-to-target connection mapping is kept in an in-memory hash table on the LB server; you don't need (and cannot use) a database, because TCP connections live on the server.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You cannot store TCP connection in a database. You just store it in memory over here

statement: When packets arrive on the source TCP connection, the load balancer looks up the mapping and forwards whatever packets it received bluntly to the target TCP connection.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: whatever TCP packets you received, you just forward them bluntly to the target TCP connection.

statement: The load balancer does not care what protocol is inside (HTTP, WebSocket, RTMP, ICMP, ...): it reads from one socket and writes to the other.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Load balancer does not care if it is HTTP, WebSocket or what not.

statement: Because the forwarded request is a well-formed HTTP request, the backend understands it, generates the response and sends it back on the TCP connection it received from; the LB server sees data on TCP 2, looks up TCP 1, forwards it, and the client gets the response.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I received from TCP 2, where do I forward it to? TCP 1.

statement: Reading from the client's socket and writing to the backend's, then reading from the backend's and writing to the client's, is exactly what a load balancer does: two lines of code.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Exactly what a load balancer does. Two lines of code and done.

statement: Another client's request gets its own pair of connections (e.g. TCP 3 to TCP 4) and is handled the same way.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: this time load balancer is connected to this one, in TCP three to TCP four.

statement: An LB server must manage 2X TCP connections (two per client request), which is why one LB server is not enough: you need multiple LB servers and horizontal scaling (a separate problem).
speaker: teacher
verbatim: the LB server needs to have two X number, requires two X number of TCP, requires to manage two X number of TCP connections

statement: You can write a single-machine load balancer locally: start a process (Go, C++, Java, Python) as the LB server on port 9000 and start backend processes on different ports of the same machine (localhost, e.g. 8081, 8082, 8083), with no cloud, VMs or Docker needed.
detail: Since one machine cannot have three processes listening on 8081, use different ports.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: just start three different processes on three different ports on the same machine.

statement: Keep a load balancing algorithm configuration; when a connection comes in, pick a backend server according to it and forward the request.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: you have the configuration as like load balancing algorithm configuration, depending on which you pick a backend server and forward the request to.

statement: Building a single-machine load balancer from first principles is really easy: it is just a mapping, 'when I get something on this TCP connection, send it to that one'; scaling is a separate matter.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When I get something from this one TCP, send it to this TCP.

statement: In the teacher's Go load balancer (lb.go), the LB server listens on port 9090 and four backend servers are hardcoded: Flask hello-world processes from the same code base on four different local ports (around 8081-8084).
detail: He wanted to test load balancing, not scale the system. Port numbers are garbled in the transcript.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I hardcoded bunch of backend servers here. You can see I have four backend servers running Flask hello world

statement: The load balancer's main loop is a small infinite for loop calling listener.Accept, which waits for an incoming client connection; the accepted TCP connection is wrapped in a 'source connection' object (with a request ID for logging) and passed to a proxy function.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I'm doing listener.Accept, which means I'm waiting. My LB server is waiting for an incoming connection.
flags: check: sentence seems cut off between 00:59:57 and 01:00:06

statement: In proxy, the first step is to pick the backend: lb.strategy.GetNextBackend returns a backend (host and port) according to the strategy (round robin, consistent hashing, ...), and the LB server dials a TCP connection to it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Our first step is to figure out which backend server to talk to.

statement: With a source connection and a backend connection, the load balancer calls copy (which copies from one file to another) twice: source to backend (request) and backend to source (response), each in its own goroutine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: copy everything you have. From source connection. To backend connection. And copy everything you get. From backend connection. To source connection.

statement: The copy call is blocking: without its own thread it would block until the connection terminates and the response would never be read, which is why each copy runs in a goroutine.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: This is a blocking call because of which I added goroutines over here.

statement: The teacher's implementation is not efficient: it spins up as many goroutines as needed.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: I have not done very efficient implementation.

statement: A load balancer like this can be implemented in about five hours with basic networking knowledge; there is no magic sauce, and everything else is the load balancing strategy.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You can literally implement it in five hours. You might just need to know basics of networking

statement: The code has round robin, static and hashed balancing strategies; round robin's GetNextBackend keeps the index of the last backend used and picks (index + 1) mod number of backends: 1 2 3, 1 2 3.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: it just does index plus one mod x back end and pick, of all the back ends pick that particular index.

statement: The consistent hashing strategy implementation is a little more complex but still simple; the teacher has a blog on it.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: That when there is a consistent hashing with implementation, that is different. So little more complex

statement: Be curious and go deep into systems: you may land in a situation where you must write a very lightweight proxy because existing proxies are not performant enough.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: You might have to just write a very lightweight proxy because existing proxies are not performant enough.

statement: The teacher's basic load balancer does not maintain connection counts; it tracks one statistic per backend, the number of requests handled so far, to verify round robin works; other statistics can be updated once a backend is picked.
detail: Student 1 asked how the connection count is decremented when a user disconnects.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: for each back end I'm keeping track of number of requests that it has handled up until now.

statement: When a connection terminates you know about it because it raises a panic/exception, which you can capture to update the load balancer's in-memory state.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: What has happened when a connection terminates, you would know about it because it would raise a panic.

statement: Between load balancer and API server there are no REST calls: it is a normal TCP connection, and the load balancer copies anything (HTTP, RPC calls, any packet) from one side to the other.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: It may send HTTP, it may send RPC calls, it may send anything. We don't really care.

statement: The copy call keeps copying continuously from one TCP connection (or file) to the other until it receives EOF.
detail: Proposed by Student 4; the teacher confirmed ('End of file') and added that copy stops once it receives EOF.
speaker: student (proposal)
verbatim: It continuously goes on happening until it receives an EOF.

statement: Copy returns only when it receives EOF, so you cannot wait on it in line; the two copies run as two goroutines in parallel, one per direction.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Once it receives EOF, it stops. So that's when this function would return.

statement: Even a CDN is implementable in hardly an hour if you know how content is served, cached and processed; it is difficult to scale, not to build.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: Even CDN is implementable. CDN implementation, hardly one hour.

statement: The CDN is covered in depth next week.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: When we go in depth of CDN next week

statement: Building and scaling are different: very few people get to scale systems, but everyone can build them locally (Docker started by someone building it locally); multiple machines are needed only for scaling, so there is no excuse not to build.
speaker: teacher
verbatim: there is a difference between building and scaling. Scaling, very few people will get a chance to do. But building, every one of us can.
